books.title: Imposter Syndrome and Other Confessions of Alejandra Kim
books.author: Patricia Park
books.ratingNote: Very strong early reader response, especially from identity-focused YA readers.
reviewSummary: Alejandra Kim feels like she’s constantly performing versions of herself—Korean at school, Latina at home, and never quite enough of either. When her carefully balanced life starts to crack, she’s forced to confront who she is beyond other people’s expectations. Readers praise the humor, emotional honesty, and specificity of the cultural experience, often describing the book as validating, sharp, and deeply relatable.

books.title: Love on Paper
books.author: Danielle Parker
books.ratingNote: Strong reception among romance and bookish YA readers.
reviewSummary: A book-loving teen finds herself caught between fiction and real-life romance as feelings complicate her carefully imagined love story. Readers enjoy the meta commentary on romance tropes and expectations, praising the warm tone and character-driven conflict. Often described as cozy, charming, and emotionally grounded.

books.title: Lia and Beckett’s Abracadabra
books.author: Amy Parks
books.ratingNote: Positive buzz for its gentle romance and mental health themes.
reviewSummary: Lia and Beckett bond over magic tricks, small-town routines, and the quiet weight of grief and anxiety. Readers praise the soft pacing and emotional tenderness, noting how the story centers healing rather than drama. Frequently described as comforting, thoughtful, and sincere.

books.title: The 9:09 Project
books.author: Mark H. Parsons
books.ratingNote: Well received for its ensemble structure.
reviewSummary: Told through the lives of students riding the same train, the novel weaves together perspectives that reveal how small moments ripple across a community. Readers appreciate the interconnected storytelling and realism, often noting how the book captures the quiet drama of everyday teen life.

books.title: My Sister’s Big Fat Indian Wedding
books.author: Sajni Patel
books.ratingNote: Popular with readers looking for humor mixed with cultural specificity.
reviewSummary: Caught in the chaos of wedding planning, family pressure, and personal doubt, a teen must navigate tradition while figuring out what she wants for herself. Readers praise the humor, food descriptions, and honest portrayal of cultural expectations. Often described as funny, heartfelt, and relatable.

books.title: How You Grow Wings
books.author: Rimma Onoseta
books.ratingNote: Readers respond strongly to its intensity.
reviewSummary: Two sisters escape an abusive home only to face new dangers and difficult moral choices. Readers often describe the novel as gripping and emotionally heavy, praising its focus on survival, agency, and complicated love between siblings.

books.title: The Day Before
books.author: Micol Ostow
books.ratingNote: Primarily enjoyed by fans of the source series.
reviewSummary: A companion novel expanding the backstories of familiar characters before major events unfold. Readers appreciate the added context and character insight, especially those already invested in the series.

books.title: Out Now: Queer We Go Again!
books.author: Saundra Mitchell (Editor)
books.ratingNote: Strong reception from anthology and queer YA readers.
reviewSummary: A collection of short stories celebrating queer joy, experimentation, and possibility across genres. Readers praise the variety of voices and tones, noting that the anthology balances fun with emotional depth.

books.title: What’s Coming to Me
books.author: Francesca Padilla
books.ratingNote: Positive response to its mix of anger and empowerment.
reviewSummary: After enduring exploitation at work, a teen plots revenge while grappling with grief and survival. Readers praise the emotional urgency and refusal to soften anger, often describing the book as cathartic and tense.

books.title: The Do-Over
books.author: Lynn Painter
books.ratingNote: Popular rom-com with strong reader enthusiasm.
reviewSummary: A teen relives the same disastrous Valentine’s Day again and again, slowly learning what—and who—actually matters. Readers enjoy the humor and fast pacing, often describing the book as fun, self-aware, and emotionally satisfying.

books.title: Consent
books.author: Nancy Ohlin
books.ratingNote: Divided but intense reader reactions.
reviewSummary: A student-teacher relationship is gradually revealed as manipulation rather than romance. Readers note the discomfort is intentional, praising the book for forcing readers to reconsider power and trust.

books.title: Lycanthropy and Other Chronic Illnesses
books.author: Kristen O’Neal
books.ratingNote: Highly appreciated for chronic illness representation.
reviewSummary: After leaving college due to Lyme disease, a teen finds connection through an online support group with unexpected truths. Readers praise the metaphor-driven storytelling and humor layered over pain.

books.title: We Are All Made of Molecules
books.author: Susin Nielsen
books.ratingNote: Consistently praised for humor and emotional intelligence.
reviewSummary: When socially awkward Stewart and popular Ashley are forced into the same blended family, their clashing perspectives reveal grief, secrecy, and unexpected empathy. Readers frequently praise the alternating narration, noting how humor softens serious themes without trivializing them. Many describe the book as laugh-out-loud funny but quietly heartbreaking, especially in how it handles loss and hidden pain.

books.title: This Is Where It Ends
books.author: Marieke Nijkamp
books.ratingNote: Strong emotional impact with heavy discussion use.
reviewSummary: Told over 54 minutes during a school shooting, the novel follows multiple students trapped inside their auditorium. Readers describe the pacing as relentless and emotionally exhausting by design. Reviews often highlight how the shifting viewpoints humanize fear, regret, and courage, making the book difficult but powerful.

books.title: Holding Up the Universe
books.author: Jennifer Niven
books.ratingNote: Very strong emotional connection with readers.
reviewSummary: Libby Strout and Jack Masselin bond while navigating grief, body image, and a neurological condition that affects face recognition. Readers praise the dual narration and emotional openness, often describing the book as affirming and tender. Reviews frequently note how the story challenges assumptions about visibility and worth.

books.title: All the Bright Places
books.author: Jennifer Niven
books.ratingNote: High engagement with mixed but intense reactions.
reviewSummary: Finch and Violet form a bond while navigating grief, depression, and the search for meaning. Readers often describe the book as beautiful but devastating, praising its portrayal of first love and mental illness. Many note that it sparks strong emotional reactions and lingering discussion.

books.title: When We Ride
books.author: Rex Ogle
books.ratingNote: Strong response to its verse format and intensity.
reviewSummary: Written in verse, the novel follows three friends whose loyalty is tested by drugs, violence, and fear. Readers praise the urgency of the language and emotional immediacy. Reviews often highlight how quickly the story escalates and how helpless the characters feel as events spiral.

books.title: ASAP
books.author: Axie Oh
books.ratingNote: Popular among fans of contemporary romance.
reviewSummary: Set in the high-pressure world of fame and ambition, the novel explores romance shaped by timing and public scrutiny. Readers praise the emotional tension and glamorous backdrop, often describing it as fast-paced and heartfelt.

books.title: XOXO
books.author: Axie Oh
books.ratingNote: Very strong popularity and reader enthusiasm.
reviewSummary: A classically trained cellist falls for a K-pop idol, forcing both to choose between love and ambition. Readers praise the escapist glamour and emotional sincerity, often highlighting the tension between personal desire and public expectation.

books.title: Asking For It
books.author: Louise O’Neill
books.ratingNote: Intense reactions and heavy discussion.
reviewSummary: After an assault goes viral, Emma becomes the subject of public scrutiny and cruelty. Readers describe the novel as brutal and unflinching, praising its refusal to soften victim-blaming. Many say it is emotionally exhausting but deeply important.

books.title: Like Home
books.author: Louisa Onomé
books.ratingNote: Strong appreciation for community-centered storytelling.
reviewSummary: Nelo watches her neighborhood change after violence draws national attention and outside intervention. Readers praise the focus on displacement, loyalty, and how media narratives flatten real communities. Often described as tense, angry, and deeply personal.

books.title: Nick and Charlie
books.author: Alice Oseman
books.ratingNote: Extremely strong fan response.
reviewSummary: Nick and Charlie face the reality of long-distance love as university approaches. Readers praise the emotional honesty and softness, often describing the novella as comforting but quietly painful. Many fans see it as a natural, realistic evolution of first love.

books.title: Radio Silence
books.author: Alice Oseman
books.ratingNote: Highly praised for its realism.
reviewSummary: Frances begins questioning her future after forming a friendship rooted in creativity rather than achievement. Readers praise the book’s critique of academic pressure and identity performance. Frequently described as validating and quietly radical.

books.title: I Was Born for This
books.author: Alice Oseman
books.ratingNote: Strong resonance with fandom culture readers.
reviewSummary: The novel explores fame from both the fan and performer perspective, highlighting anxiety, pressure, and identity. Readers praise the dual viewpoint and emotional authenticity, often noting how accurately it captures modern fandom.

books.title: Solitaire
books.author: Alice Oseman
books.ratingNote: Mixed but thoughtful reader response.
reviewSummary: Following Tori Spring, the novel examines numbness, cynicism, and quiet depression. Readers often describe it as darker and more introspective than Oseman’s later works. Many appreciate its honesty even when it feels uncomfortable.

books.title: Anger Is a Gift
books.author: Mark Oshiro
books.ratingNote: Strong engagement driven by political relevance.
reviewSummary: After repeated trauma at school and in his community, Moss must decide whether anger will destroy him or empower change. Readers praise the urgency and emotional clarity, often describing the book as raw, validating, and galvanizing.
